# Infinitely divisible privacy and beyond I resolution of the $s^{2}=2k$ conjecture

**Authors:** Aaradhya Pandey Affiliation: Princeton University Arian Maleki Affiliation: Columbia University Sanjeev Kulkarni Affiliation: Princeton University

## Abstract

Differential privacy is increasingly formalized through the lens of hypothesis testing via the robust and interpretable $f$ -DP framework, where privacy guarantees are encoded by a baseline Blackwell trade-off function $f_{\infty}=T(P_{\infty},Q_{\infty})$ involving a pair of distributions $(P_{\infty},Q_{\infty})$ Dong et al. (2022). The problem of ‘choosing the right privacy metric in practice’ Cummings and collaborators (2024) gives rise to a central question in this framework: what is a statistically appropriate baseline $f_{\infty}$ given some prior modeling assumptions? The special case of Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) Dong et al. (2022) showed that, under compositions of nearly perfect DP mechanisms, these baseline trade-off functions exhibit a central limit behavior: $f_{n}=T(P_{n}^{\otimes n},Q_{n}^{\otimes n})\to f_{\infty}=T(P_{\infty},Q_{\infty})$ , where the limiting baseline trade-off function $f_{\infty}$ involves two shifted Gaussians $P_{\infty},Q_{\infty}$ . Inspired by Le Cam’s theory of limits of statistical experiments Le Cam (1986), we answer this question in full generality in its natural infinitely divisible setting.

We show that the sequence of composition experiments $(P_{n}^{\otimes n},Q_{n}^{\otimes n})$ ‘converge’ in general to a binary limit experiment $(P_{\infty},Q_{\infty})$ whose log-likelihood ratio $\log\frac{dQ_{\infty}}{dP_{\infty}}$ is an infinitely divisible distribution under the limiting null $P_{\infty}$ . So, any such limiting trade-off function $f_{\infty}$ involves an infinitely divisible law $P_{\infty}$ characterized by its Lévy–Khintchine triplet, and its Esscher tilt $dQ_{\infty}(x)=e^{x}dP_{\infty}(x)$ . As a consequence, we determine all the limiting baseline trade-off functions $f_{\infty}$ under the composition of nearly perfect differentially private procedures. Our framework recovers GDP as the purely Gaussian case, yields explicit many non-Gaussian limits including Poisson, and many others. Consequently, we positively resolve the $s^{2}=2k$ conjecture proposed in the GDP paper Dong et al. (2022), which curiously observed that in the Gaussian examples $P_{\infty}\overset{d}{=}-k+|s|Z$ with $Z\sim N(0,1)$ , we always have $s^{2}=2k$ . Then, we describe situations where one can goes beyond the infinite divisibility framework, such as $\log\frac{dQ_{\infty}}{dP_{\infty}}$ being a Gaussian mixture under $P_{\infty}$ . Finally, we describe a mechanism for count statistics that optimally achieves (asymmetric) Poisson differentially privacy, going beyond the natural noise-adding mechanisms used in practice.

## 1 Introduction, previous work, and our contributions

Modern data analysis routinely draws on information about people: their location traces, search histories, media consumption, social graphs, alongside long-standing, highly sensitive records from hospitals, schools, and national censuses. This necessarily demands a framework of data analysis that preserves the privacy of individuals. Early privacy practices leaned on ad-hoc anonymization, but a series of high-profile re-identifications made it clear that simple de-identification is brittle at scale Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008). This motivated a rigorous foundation for privacy in statistical analysis. Differential privacy (DP) provides exactly that: a principled, mathematically verifiable guarantee against disclosure risks that persists under arbitrary post-processing and composition. Since its introduction, differential privacy has grown into a practical standard, with widespread industrial adoption Apple Inc. (2017) and deployment in official statistics Abowd (2018).

### 1.1 From $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ and divergence based DP to Hypothesis testing based DP

In its classical form, differential privacy formalizes protection via two real-valued parameters $\varepsilon\geq 0$ , $0\leq\delta\leq 1$ , which jointly bound the advantage of any adversary attempting to distinguish between neighboring datasets from a mechanism’s output Dwork et al. (2006a); Dwork et al. (2006b). The $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ formulation of differential privacy became the standard due to its robustness to post-processing, group privacy, and composability, but sharp accounting under composition proved to be technically delicate Dwork and Roth (2014). A line of divergence-based relaxations was subsequently developed to tighten composition analyses and enable modular accounting: concentrated DP (CDP and zCDP) Dwork and Rothblum (2016) Bun and Steinke (2016), and Rényi DP (RDP) Mironov (2017), with follow-ups on amplification by subsampling and analytic accountants Wang et al. (2019); Abadi et al. (2016).

In parallel, a practical, robust, and interpretable hypothesis-testing viewpoint of differential privacy was formalized, starting with Wasserman and Zhou (2010) and Kairouz et al. (2015). It describes privacy as the hypothesis testing problem of distinguishing between two neighboring datasets $S,S^{\prime}$ via the output distributions $M(S),M(S^{\prime})$ of a private mechanism $M$ . This was formalized in the framework of $f$ -differential privacy ( $f$ -DP) Dong et al. (2022), which describes privacy of $M$ by requiring that the optimal type I vs type II error curve for the distinguishing test for $M(S),M(S^{\prime})$ , for any two neighboring datasets, $S$ and $S^{\prime}$ , stays above a baseline trade-off function (TOF) $f$ .

Immediately, the $f$ -DP framework is statistically interpretable via hypothesis testing. It recovers the classical $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ -DP formulation for a certain choice of baseline trade-off function $f_{\varepsilon,\delta}$ Wasserman and Zhou (2010)11 1 The expression of $f_{\varepsilon,\delta}$ is given by $f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\alpha)=\max\left(0,1-\delta-e^{\varepsilon}\alpha,e^{-\varepsilon}(1-\delta-\alpha)\right)$ for $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ., and it is a robust framework because it uniformly preserves privacy at all scales of type $I$ error $0\leq\alpha\leq 1$ . Moreover, it is achievable by appropriate noise injection mechanisms Awan and Vadhan (2023)22 2 Although very general, the noise adding mechanisms described here are not quite naturally implementable., and it is closed and tight under composition, thereby allowing for lossless reasoning about composition Dong et al. (2022). Finally, Dong et al. (2022) introduced Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) as a one-parameter family of baseline trade-off curves $G_{\mu}$ that require distinguishing between a pair of shifted normal distributions $N\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)$ and $N\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)$ with the same variance $\mu^{2}$ for a real-valued parameter $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ 33 3 From the basic symmetries of Gaussian trade-off functions $G_{\mu}$ Pandey et al. (2025), our description of $G_{\mu}$ is equivalent to the usual description of itself involving the pair of distributions $N(0,1)$ and $N(\mu,1)$ . However, our formulation will make the resolution of the $s^{2}=2k$ conjecture of Dong et al. (2022) appear naturally. and showed that it optimally captures the widely used Gaussian mechanism. Dong et al. (2022) further showed that under compositions of nearly perfect DP mechanisms $M_{n}\otimes\cdots\otimes M_{1}$ , these baseline trade-off functions $f_{n}\otimes\cdots\otimes f_{1}$ converge to a limiting baseline trade-off function $G_{\mu}$ involving two shifted Gaussians as above.

### 1.2 Our contribution: In search of a baseline trade-off function

Dong et al. (2022) established a central limit behavior within differential privacy, indicating that the baseline trade off function $f$ should be chosen as a trade off function $T(P_{\infty},Q_{\infty})$ (see definition 1) for a shifted Gaussian pair $P_{\infty}=N\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)$ and $Q_{\infty}=N\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)$ , for some $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ under a larger number of (nearly perfect) differentially private outputs based on queries on the same dataset.

- • An infinitely divisible framework of privacy. In this paper, we generalize this result in its natural infinitely divisible setting (see Theorem 6) and establish that under a large number of (nearly perfect) differentially private operations, if the deteriorated trade-off curves converge to a limiting trade-off curve, then the limiting trade-off curve has an infinitely divisible form (see Equation (18)), encompassing both Gaussian and Poisson components44 4 Inspired by Le Cam and Yang (2000) ‘The gaussian ones are used everywhere because of mathematical tractability. Poisson experiments are less tractable and less studied, but they are probably more important. They will loom large in the new century.’, and given that we are in the next century, we show how the Poisson baselines are extremely relevant for differentially private analysis on graph based relational datasets..

- • Resolution of the $s^{2}=2k$ conjecture. As an application of Theorem 6, we resolve the $s^{2}=2k$ conjecture (see Theorem 3) proposed in Dong et al. (2022), which observed that in the Gaussian case $P_{\infty}\overset{d}{=}-k+|s|Z$ with $Z\sim N(0,1)$ , we always have $s^{2}=2k$ .

- • Random number of operations and beyond infinite divisibility. In practice, we do not know the number of differentially private operations one is going the implement on the same dataset. In section 3.1 (see Equation (64)) we derive that under a large but random number of (nearly perfect) differentially private operations, the limiting trade-off functions can go beyond the class of infinitely divisible trade-off functions. Inspired by Le Cam (1986), we demonstrate this with a locally asymptotically mixed normal example 66.

- • Achieving Poisson differential privacy in practice. In Theorem 13 , we describe a mechanism that optimally achieves (asymmetric) Poisson differential privacy real-valued statistics, including count statistics with baseline privacy $f=T(P(\lambda_{1}),P(\lambda_{2}))$ going beyond the popular noise -adding mechanisms.

- • Applications to graph-based relational datasets. We demonstrate how Poisson differential privacy becomes extremely relevant in tightly capturing privacy on datasets that are relational or graph-based and only allow released statistics to be inherently discretized 4.

- • A coarsened Neyman-Pearson lemma. Inspired by a Bayesian perspective of differential privacy Strack and Yang (2024), we prove (see Theorem 22) exactly how the trade-off functions $T(P,Q)$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ degrade when we shrink the underlying the $\sigma$ -algebra of information from $\mathcal{F}$ to $\mathcal{G}$ , and demonstrate with a Gaussian example55 5 The results extend with appropriate modifications for any symmetric log concave shift family on $\mathbb{R}$ . (see Proposition 2).

## 2 Hypothesis Testing-Based Privacy: Definitions and Motivations

We describe objects of the hypothesis-testing-based privacy framework and motivate our problem.

### 2.1 Basics of trade-off functions and Blackwell ordering

#### Definition 1 (Trade-off function Dong et al. (2022)).

Given two probability distributions $P,Q$ on a measurable space $(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}})$ , we define the trade-off function as the map $=T(P,Q):[0,1]\to[0,1]$

$$ T(P,Q)(\alpha):=\inf_{\varphi}\Bigl\{\beta_{\varphi}:=\mathbb{E}_{Q}[1-\varphi]\,\Bigm|\,\alpha_{\varphi}:=\mathbb{E}_{P}[\varphi]\leq\alpha,\;\varphi:(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}})\!\to[0,1]\text{ measurable}\Bigr\}. $$

Intuition, the Neyman-Pearson optimizer. For any type I error $\alpha\in[0,1]$ , the trade-off function (TOF) returns the smallest value of type II error $\beta_{\varphi}$ over all possible Borel measurable test functions $\varphi\colon\mathcal{W}\to[0,1]$ . As a consequence of Neyman-Pearson lemma Polyanskiy and Wu (2025)[Thm 14.11] $T(P,Q)(\alpha)$ is achieved by the following likelihood ratio test for every $\alpha\in[0,1]$

$$ \varphi^{*}(w):=\mathbf{1}\left(\frac{dQ}{d\mu}>\tau^{*}\frac{dP}{d\mu}\right)+\lambda^{*}\mathbf{1}\left(\frac{dQ}{d\mu}=\tau^{*}\frac{dP}{d\mu}\right),\quad\frac{dQ}{dP}:=\frac{dQ}{d\mu}/\frac{dP}{d\mu}:(\Omega,\mathcal{F})\to[0,\infty] $$

for $2\mu=P+Q$ , are the ratio of Radon–Nikodym derivatives, and $\tau^{*},\lambda^{*}$ are determined as follows. Choose $\tau^{*}\in[0,\infty]$ as the unique number66 6 Such a $\tau^{*}$ uniquely exists as the CDF $F:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1],$ defined as $F(t):=P\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}\leq t\right)$ is monotone increasing as a function of $t$ satisfying $(t_{1}\leq t_{2}\rightarrow F(t_{1})\leq F(t_{2}))$ , right continuous ( $\lim_{t\downarrow t_{0}}F(t)=F(t_{0})$ ) with $F(0^{-})=P_{0}\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}<0\right)=0$ (lower limit of $\alpha$ ) and $\lim_{t\to\infty}F(t)=1$ (upper limit of $\alpha$ ). such that $P\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}\geq\tau^{*}\right)\geq\alpha\geq P\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}>\tau^{*}\right)$ , and

$$ \text{define }\lambda^{*}:=\frac{\alpha-P\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}>\tau^{*}\right)}{P\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}\geq\tau^{*}\right)-P\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}>\tau^{*}\right)}\mathbf{1}\left(\alpha-P\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}>\tau^{*}\right)>0\right)\text{ to have }\mathbb{E}_{P}[\varphi^{*}]=\alpha. $$

Characterization of TOFS and their inverse. Dong et al. (2022)[Prop 1] proved that the collection of all trade-off functions $\mathcal{T}:=\{T(P,Q):(P,Q)\text{ on some measurable }(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}})\}$ is the same as77 7 As argued in Torgersen (1991) and is also immediate that the set $\mathcal{T}$ says the same, if we keep all the conditions intact, except one, where we replace the condition $f(x)\leq 1-x$ for all $x\in[0,1]$ by just $f(1)=0$ .

$$ \mathcal{T}=\{f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\text{ convex, continuous, decreasing and }f(\alpha)\leq 1-\alpha\text{ for all }\alpha\in[0,1]\} $$

Moreover, any such $f\in\mathcal{T}$ can be realized as $T(P,Q)$ on $\mathcal{W}=[0,1],\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}}=\mathcal{B}_{[0,1]}$ by taking $P$ to be the standard uniform probability measure $U$ on $([0,1],\mathcal{B}_{[0,1]})$ and $Q=Q_{f}$ to be a Borel probability measure on $[0,1]$ with cumulative distribution function $Q([0,x])=f(1-x)$ for $x\in[0,1)$ and having an atom at $x=1$ of mass $Q(\{1\})=1-f(0)$ whenever $f(0)<1$ . Finally, if $f=T(P,Q)$ then its generalized inverse is a trade off function and $f^{-1}=T(Q,P)$ Dong et al. (2022)[Lem A.2]

$$ \text{ where }f^{-1}:[0,1]\to[0,1]\text{ defined as }f^{-1}(\alpha)=\inf\{t\in[0,1]:f(t)\leq\alpha\}\text{ for }\alpha\in[0,1]. $$

Functional ordering and indistinguishability (privacy). One can define a functional ordering

$$ \textbf{Blackwell ordering:}\quad T(P^{\prime},Q^{\prime})(\alpha)\geq T(P,Q)(\alpha)\text{ for all }\alpha\in[0,1] $$

capturing the intuition that the pair of distributions $(P^{\prime},Q^{\prime})$ defined on some space $(\mathcal{W}^{\prime},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}^{\prime}})$ is more difficult to distinguish from a sample than the pair $(P,Q)$ defined on another space $(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}})$ , uniformly across every scale $0\leq\alpha\leq 1$ . We refer to Torgersen (1991) for a comprehensive treatment of equivalent conditions for this ordering also known as Blackwell-Le-Cam equivalence.

Blackwell ordering. Further, the functional ordering $f\geq g$ for $f,g\in\mathcal{T}$ (a partial ordering on $\mathcal{T}$ since not all pairs are comparable) described above is equivalent to the Blackwell ordering Dong et al. (2022)[Thm 2]. More precisely, $T(P^{\prime},Q^{\prime})(\alpha)\geq T(P,Q)(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha\in[0,1]$ if and only if there exists a Markov kernel $R:\mathcal{W}\to\mathcal{W}^{\prime}$ Kallenberg (2021) such that $(P^{\prime},Q^{\prime})=(R(P),R(Q))$ .

### 2.2 Basics of $f$ -differential privacy, motivation of our work

In this subsection, we introduce the f-differential privacy framework of Dong et al. (2022) based on Blackwell ordering and specialize to Gaussian differential privacy to motivate our generalization. Along the way, inspired by Torgersen (1991), we also state an equivalent way of describing the $f$ -differential privacy of Dong et al. (2022) through their minimum Bayes risks.

#### Definition 2 ( $f$ -differential privacy Dong et al. (2022)).

For $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ , given an input space $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}})$ and an output space $(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}})$ , a Markov kernel (randomized mechanism) $M:\mathcal{X}^{k}\to\mathcal{Y}$ is said to satisfy $f$ -DP for some trade off function $f\in\mathcal{T}$ if minimizing over neighboring datasets $S,S^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}^{k}$ 88 8 Instead of the product metric space $(\mathcal{X}^{k},d_{H})$ with the Hamming metric $d_{H}(\underline{x},\underline{y})=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbf{1}(x_{i}\neq y_{i})$ , one can consider any metric space $(\mathcal{X},d)$ with the appropriate change in definitions. See 12 for more.

$$ \inf_{d_{H}(S,S^{\prime})\leq 1}T\big(M(S),M(S^{\prime}))\big)\;\geq\;f\quad\text{pointwise on }[0,1]. $$

$k$ dependence, intuition, post processing. For different values of $k$ , one has different Markov kernels $M(k)$ and can allow different baseline trade off functions $f_{k}\in\mathcal{T}$ . Let $f=T(P,Q)$ for probability measures $P,Q$ on a space $(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}})$ . Then the above definition captures the intuition that distinguishing the outputs of $M$ for any neighboring $S,S^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}^{k}$ is at least as hard as distinguishing between a sample of $P$ or $Q$ . Moreover, if $M:\mathcal{X}^{k}\to\mathcal{Y}$ is $f$ -DP and $R:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z}$ is a Markov kernel independent of the data given $M$ , then $R\circ M:\mathcal{X}^{k}\to\mathcal{Z}$ is also $f$ -DP Dong et al. (2022).

Convex duality and connections to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ -DP and others. It follows from definition that if a Markov kernel $M$ satisfy $f_{i}$ DP for all $i\in I$ , then it satisfy $\sup_{i\in I}f_{i}$ DP. Moreover, Wasserman and Zhou (2010) established that satisfying $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ -DP in the classical sense is equivalent to satisfying $f_{\varepsilon,\delta}$ -DP in the sense above, with $f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\alpha)=\max(0,1-\delta-e^{\varepsilon}\alpha,e^{-\varepsilon}(1-\delta-\alpha))$ for $\alpha\in[0,1]$ . As a consequence of the two above and convex duality99 9 A convex, continuous $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ is the pointwise supremum of all affine functions lying below it., for a symmetric trade off function $f=f^{-1}$ we have a Markov kernel $M$ satisfy $f$ -DP if and only if it satisfy $(\varepsilon,\delta(\varepsilon))$ -DP in the classical sense, for all $\varepsilon\geq 0$ with $\delta(\varepsilon)=1+f^{*}(-e^{\varepsilon})$ , where $f^{*}(y)=\sup_{\alpha\in[0,1]}(\alpha y-f(\alpha))$ is the convex conjugate of $f$ . We refer to Dong et al. (2022)[Appendix B] for the conversion of $f$ -DP to divergence-based DP. Inspired by Torgersen (1991), one can derive a duality relation between the trade-off curve

$$ f(\alpha)=T(P,Q)(\alpha)=\inf_{\varphi}\Bigl\{\mathbb{E}_{Q}[1-\varphi]\,\Bigm|\,\mathbb{E}_{P}[\varphi]\leq\alpha,\;\varphi:(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}})\!\to[0,1]\text{ measurable}\Bigr\}, $$

and the minimum Bayes risk for the testing problem $(P,Q)$ with prior $(1-\lambda,\lambda)$ for $\lambda\in[0,1]$

$$ b(\lambda)=B(P,Q)(\alpha)=\min_{\varphi}\Bigl\{(1-\lambda)\mathbb{E}_{P}[\varphi]+\lambda\mathbb{E}_{Q}[1-\varphi]\,\Bigm|\ \varphi:(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}})\!\to[0,1]\text{ measurable}\Bigr\}. $$

The precise duality relation for the pair of functions $f,b:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ is given by1010 10 This representation writes out $f$ as a suprema over linear functions $f(\alpha)=\sup_{0<\lambda\leq 1}\Big[\frac{b(\lambda)}{\lambda}-\frac{(1-\lambda)}{\lambda}\alpha\Big],$

$$ f(\alpha)=\sup_{0<\lambda\leq 1}\Bigg[\frac{b(\lambda)-(1-\lambda)\alpha}{\lambda}\Bigg],\quad b(\lambda)=\inf_{0\leq\alpha\leq 1}\Bigg[(1-\lambda)\alpha+\lambda f(\alpha)\Bigg]. $$

The equivalence between $f\leftrightarrow b$ gives rise to the an enumeration of all such functions $\{B(P,Q):[0,1]\to[0,1]:(P,Q)\text{ probability measures on some }(\Omega,\mathcal{F})\}$ as the following class.

$$ \mathcal{B}:=\{b:[0,1]\to[0,1]\quad|\quad b\text{ concave and }b(\lambda)\leq\min(\lambda,1-\lambda)\text{ for all }\lambda\in[0,1]\} $$

Moreover, Blackwell ordering $f_{1}\geq f_{2}$ for $f_{1},f_{2}\in\mathcal{T}$ can be equivalently stated in terms of their corresponding minimum Bayes risks $b_{1}\geq b_{2}$ , pointwise on $[0,1]$ . So, the entire framework of $f$ -differential privacy proposed in Dong et al. (2022) can also be written equivalently in terms of the minimum Bayes risk function $b$ . However, working with $b$ has the advantage that $b$ is affine under mixtures of experiments. More precisely, given pairs of binary (Blackwell-Le-Cam) experiments $\mathcal{E}_{1}=(\Omega_{1},\mathcal{F}_{1},P_{1},Q_{1})$ and $\mathcal{E}_{2}=(\Omega_{2},\mathcal{F}_{2},P_{2},Q_{2})$ , consider the mixture experiment1111 11 The intuition is that in practice the mixture experiment is performed by deciding with probabilities $(\delta,1-\delta)$ whether to perform a sample from $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ or $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ and then a sample is drawn. The output of the experiment has the form $(I,X_{I})$ , where $I$ is the index {1, 2} of which experiment is performed and $X_{I}$ is the sample itself.

$$ \delta\mathcal{E}_{1}+(1-\delta)\mathcal{E}_{2}:=(\Omega_{1}\bigsqcup\Omega_{2},\sigma(\mathcal{F}_{1}\sqcup\mathcal{F}_{2}),\delta P_{1}+(1-\delta)P_{2},\delta Q_{1}+(1-\delta)Q_{2}). $$

$$ \text{Then }B(\delta P_{1}+(1-\delta)P_{2},\delta P_{1}+(1-\delta)P_{2})\equiv\delta B(P_{1},Q_{1})+(1-\delta)B(P_{2},Q_{2}). $$

This affineness of the functional $B$ is of importance in the sense that one can restrict the analysis of experiments that are only supported on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})\equiv(\{0,1\},2^{\{0,1\}})$ . It would be interesting to see the consequences of this in the practice of formalizing differential privacy through the $b$ function.

$G_{\mu}$ -DP and motivation of our work. A central question in this hypothesis testing-based $f$ -DP framework is to choose a statistically appropriate baseline trade-off function $f$ depending on the situation at hand. As a consequence of a central limit behavior, the focus of the paper Dong et al. (2022) was on the special case of a mechanism $M$ satisfying $G_{\mu}$ -DP by letting the baseline trade off function $f=G_{\mu}=T(P,Q)$ where $P=N\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)$ and $Q=N\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)$ for some $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ . Our motivation is to search for a universal list of baseline TOFs $f=T(P,Q)$ beyond the Gaussian one.

### 2.3 Composition and beyond the universal central limit behaviour

Now, our interests are in quantifying how privacy degrades when we compose a sequence of mechanisms $M_{1},\cdots,M_{n}$ on a (fixed) private data set $S\in\mathcal{X}^{k}$ in which each analysis is informed by prior analyses on the same data set, and more and more analysis is publicly released with increasing $n$ . For simplicity, we keep the $\sigma$ -algebras and the measurability conditions implicit in definitions.

#### Definition 3 (Composition of private mechanisms Dong et al. (2022), Kallenberg (2021)).

Consider a Markov kernel $M_{1}:\mathcal{X}^{k}\to\mathcal{Y}_{1}$ , and conditional on the following pair (data, first output) = $(S,M_{1}(S))$ , let $M_{2}:\mathcal{X}^{k}\times\mathcal{Y}_{1}\to\mathcal{Y}_{2}$ be another Markov kernel. The joint Markov kernel (randomized mechanism) $M=(M_{1},M_{2}):\mathcal{X}^{k}\to\mathcal{Y}_{1}\times\mathcal{Y}_{2}$ is defined is $M(S)=(M_{1}(S),M_{2}(S,M_{1}(S)))$ .

Intuition and $n$ step generalization. Given the dataset $S$ , the distribution of output of the joint mechanism $M(S)$ is constructed from the marginal distribution of $M_{1}(S)$ on $Y_{1}$ and the conditional distribution of $M_{2}(S,y_{1})$ on $Y_{2}$ given $M_{1}(S)=y_{1}$ . More generally, given a sequence of Markov kernels $M_{i}:\mathcal{X}^{k}\times\mathcal{Y}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{Y}_{i-1}\to\mathcal{Y}_{i}$ , we can recursively define the joint mechanism as their composition $M=(M_{1},\cdots,M_{n}):\mathcal{X}^{k}\to\mathcal{Y}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{Y}_{n}$ . Now, with increasing $n$ , we publicly release more and more analysis of the dataset $S$ , first $M_{1}(S)$ then $M_{2}(S,M_{1}(S))$ , then $M_{3}(S,M_{1}(S),M_{2}(S,M_{1}(S)))$ , and continue. The key question of how the privacy degrades as the number of analyses increases, namely under composition leads us to the following definition.

#### Definition 4 (Tensor product Dong et al. (2022)).

Consider trade off functions $f=T(P,Q)$ for probability measures $(P,Q)$ on some space $(\mathcal{W},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}})$ and $g=T(P^{\prime},Q^{\prime})$ for probability measures $(P^{\prime},Q^{\prime})$ on some space $(\mathcal{W}^{\prime},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}^{\prime}})$ . We define the tensor product trade off function as $f\otimes g:=T(P\otimes P^{\prime},Q\otimes Q^{\prime})$ , where $(P\otimes P^{\prime},Q\otimes Q^{\prime})$ are the product measures on $(\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{W}^{\prime},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}}\otimes\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{W}^{\prime}})$ .

Well-definedness and basic properties. By definition $f\otimes g$ is a trade-off function. Dong et al. (2022)[Lem C.2] showed that $f\otimes g$ is well defined in the sense that if $f=T(P,Q)=T(\tilde{P},\tilde{Q})$ , then $T(P\otimes P^{\prime},Q\otimes Q^{\prime})=T(\tilde{P}\otimes P^{\prime},\tilde{Q}\otimes Q^{\prime})$ . Moreover, we have Dong et al. Now, we state the celebrated composition theorem that tightly quantifies the privacy degradation of sequential mechanisms with the tensor product construction of trade off functions.

#### Theorem 1 (Tightest composition theorem).

Dong et al. (2022)[Thm 4] For $1\leq i\leq n$ consider Markov kernels $M_{i}$ as above so that $M_{i}(\cdot,y_{1},\cdots,y_{i-1}):\mathcal{X}^{k}\to\mathcal{Y}_{i}$ satisfy $f_{i}$ -DP for all $y_{1}\in\mathcal{Y}_{1},\cdots,y_{i-1}\in\mathcal{Y}_{i-1}$ . Before stating a central limit behavior of nearly perfect private mechanisms as the number of compositions $n\uparrow\infty$ , we need to define a few moment functionals of the log-likelihood ratio (LLR) of $P$ and $Q$ such that $f=T(P,Q)$ . The functionals $\text{kl}(f)$ $:=$ $-\int_{0}^{1}\log|f^{\prime}(x)|dx,\kappa_{2}(f):=$ $\int_{0}^{1}\log^{2}|f^{\prime}(x)|dx,\kappa_{3}(f):=$ $\int_{0}^{1}\big|\log|f^{\prime}(x)|\big|^{3}dx,\overline{\kappa}_{3}(f):=$ $\int_{0}^{1}\big|\log|f^{\prime}(x)|+\text{kl}(f)\big|^{3}dx$ (this one requires $\text{kl}(f)<\infty$ ) take values in $[0,+\infty]$ . Now, consider a triangular array of Markov kernels (randomized mechanisms) $\{M_{n1},\ldots,M_{nn}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ where $M_{ni}$ satisfy $f_{ni}$ -DP for $1\leq i\leq n$ 2.

#### Theorem 2.

Dong et al. (2022)[Thm 6] Let $\{f_{ni}:1\leq i\leq n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be a triangular array of symmetric $(f=f^{-1})$ trade-off functions and assume for constants $k\geq 0$ and $s>0$ as $n\to\infty$ we have $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\text{kl}(f_{ni})\to k,\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\text{kl}(f_{ni})\to 0,\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_{2}(f_{ni})\to s^{2},\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_{3}(f_{ni})\to 0.$ Then,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}f_{n1}\otimes\cdots\otimes f_{nn}(\alpha)=G_{2k/s}(\alpha)\text{ uniformly for all }\alpha\in[0,1]. $$

The above theorem shows (under its assumptions) that the composition of nearly perfect DP mechanisms $M_{n1}\otimes\cdots\otimes M_{nn}$ asymptotically satisfy $G_{2k/s}$ -DP, where $G_{\mu}=T\left(N\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right),N\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)\right)$ . But, consider the baseline TOFs $f_{ni}=T\left(\text{Ber}\left(\frac{\lambda_{1}}{n}\right),\text{Ber}\left(\frac{\lambda_{2}}{n}\right)\right)$ for $i\in[n]$ , then it follows from the Neyman-Pearson lemma (2) and law of small numbers that uniformly for all $\alpha\in[0,1]$ (see Corollary 9)

$$ \displaystyle f_{n1}\otimes\cdots\otimes f_{nn}(\alpha)=T\left(\text{Ber}\left(\frac{\lambda_{1}}{n}\right)^{\otimes n},\text{Ber}\left(\frac{\lambda_{2}}{n}\right)^{\otimes n}\right)(\alpha) \displaystyle=T\left(\text{Bin}\left(n,\frac{\lambda_{1}}{n}\right),\text{Bin}\left(n,\frac{\lambda_{2}}{n}\right)\right)(\alpha)\to T(P(\lambda_{1}),P(\lambda_{2}))(\alpha), $$

where $P(\lambda_{1}),P(\lambda_{2})$ denotes Poisson distributions with mean $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ for some $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>0$ . This example is clearly beyond the reach of the framework of Gaussian differential privacy, and depicts that based on the situation at hand, the baseline trade-off functions could be non-Gaussian. We unify Gaussian and Poisson limits under the framework of infinite divisibility Janssen et al. (1985).

On the $s^{2}=2k$ conjecture of Dong et al. (2022). It was remarked in Dong et al. (2022) that ‘in all examples of the application of Theorem 2’ it is observed that $s^{2}=2k$ . We resolve this conjecture positively in our infinitely divisible setting as a consequence of a contiguity requirement.

### 2.4 Infinitely divisible distributions and Lévy-Khintchine formula

Now, we define infinitely divisible distributions, give some examples, state basic properties including closure under scaling and convolution, and weak limits, describe their appearances as distributional limits of sums of triangular arrays of (row-wise) IID random variables Kallenberg (2021).

#### Definition 5 (Infinitely divisible distribution (IDD)).

A random variable $X$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is called infinitely divisible if $\forall$ $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ , there exists IID random variables $X_{n1},\cdots,X_{nn}$ such that $X\overset{d}{=}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{ni}$ .

Equivalent definitions. A probability measure $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})$ or its (equivalent) Fourier transform $\hat{\mu}(t)=\mu(e^{itx})$ for $t\in\mathbb{R}$ is called infinitely divisible if for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ , there exists a probability measure (which is also unique) $\mu_{n}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})$ such that $\mu=\mu_{n}^{*n}$ or equivalently $\hat{\mu}(t)=\hat{\mu}_{n}(t)^{n}$ for $t\in\mathbb{R}$ , where $\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)d\mu*\nu(x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}f(x+y)d\mu(x)d\nu(y)$ defines the convolution of measures $\mu*\nu$ by varying $f$ . We denote with $\mathcal{I}$ the collection of all infinitely divisible distributions on $\mathbb{R}$ .

Intuition, Gaussian and Compound Poisson examples in $\mathcal{I}$ . The notion of infinitely divisible distribution captures the intuition that the random variable $X$ can be broken into smaller IID pieces of arbitrary order. Elements of $\mathcal{I}$ include Normal distribution $\mu_{1}\overset{d}{=}m+\sigma Z\leftrightarrow\hat{\mu}_{1}(t)=e^{itm-\frac{t^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}},t\in\mathbb{R}$ for some $m,\sigma\in\mathbb{R}$ , Compound Poisson distribution $\mu_{2}\overset{d}{=}\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}$ , with IID $X_{i}\sim\frac{\nu}{\|\nu\|}$ for $i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ and independent $N\sim P(\|\nu\|)\perp\{X_{i}\}_{i\geq 1}$ , where $\nu$ is a (uniquely determined from $\mu_{2}$ ) positive finite Borel measure on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ of total mass $\|\nu\|=\nu(\mathbb{R})$ $\leftrightarrow\log\hat{\mu}_{2}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}(e^{itx}-1)d\nu(x)$ . One can also represent the measure $\mu_{2}(\nu)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}}e^{-\nu(\mathbb{R})}\frac{\nu^{*k}}{k!}$ as a Poisson mixture of measures.

Basic closure properties of $\mathcal{I}$ . $\mathcal{I}$ is closed under some algebraic properties including affine change: $\mathcal{I}\ni X$ implies $c_{1}X+c_{2}\in\mathcal{I}$ for $c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}$ , convolution: $X_{1}\perp X_{2}\in\mathcal{I}$ implies $X=X_{1}+X_{2}\in\mathcal{I}$ . As a consequence we have an independent sum of Gaussian and Compound Poisson $X=m+\sigma Z+\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}$ as described above, is also infinitely divisible. $\mathcal{I}$ is also closed under analytic properties including weak convergence: $\mathcal{I}\ni\mu_{n}\overset{d}{\to}\mu$ implies $\mu\in\mathcal{I}$ . Consequently, Poisson, Geometric, Negative Binomial, as well as Chi-square, Exponential, Gamma, and Cauchy are all elements of $\mathcal{I}$ . Moreover, a probability measure $\mu$ on $(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})$ is infinitely divisible if and only if there is a sequence of positive finite Borel measures $\{\nu_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}}$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ so that $\mu_{2}(\nu_{n})\overset{d}{\to}\mu$ Kallenberg (2021).

Generalization of CLT and parametrizing limits as elements of IDD. A remarkable generalization of the central limit theorem says if $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})$ is such that there exists a triangular array of (row-wise) IID random variables $\{X_{ni}:1\leq i\leq n\}_{n\geq 1}$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{ni}\overset{d}{\to}\mu$ , then $\mu\in\mathcal{I}$ Durrett (2019), Bose et al. (2002). In fact, something more general holds, where one can drop the identically distributed condition 1212 12 We still keep the independence of elements of the row $\{X_{ni}:1\leq i\leq n\}$ for every row. on the triangular array, and replace it with a weaker condition on the triangular array also known as the uniformly asymptotically negligible condition given by

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\mathbb{P}[|X_{ni}|\geq\varepsilon]=0\text{ for all }\varepsilon>0 $$

Even under such weaker row-wise independent triangular array, $\{X_{ni}:1\leq i\leq n\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}}$ , if $\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{ni}\overset{d}{\to}\mu$ , then $\mu\in\mathcal{I}$ Klenke (2008). This enumeration of all possible limit distributions as elements of $\mathcal{I}$ is also the key technical ingredient of our enumeration of all possible baseline trade-off functions. We will establish our results again in two such stages like the above.

Lévy-Khintchine representation of IDD. Every IDD $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has a unique Lévy-Khintchine parametrization $(m,\sigma,\nu)$ of their Fourier transform with Gaussian and Compound Poisson parts, with $\nu$ a positive Borel measure on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ satisfying $\int_{\mathbb{R}}(x^{2}\wedge 1)d\nu(x)<\infty$ Kallenberg (2021)

$$ \log\hat{\mu}(t)=itm-\frac{1}{2}t^{2}\sigma^{2}+\int_{\mathbb{R}}(e^{itx}-1-itx\mathbf{1}(|x|\leq 1))d\nu(x). $$

Kolmogorov series representation of IDD. Consider $m\in\mathbb{R},\sigma\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ . Then one can define

$$ X=m+\sigma Z+X_{0}+\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}}(X_{k}-\mathbb{E}[X_{k}]) $$

a random series with independent random variables $Z\overset{d}{=}N(0,1)$ , $X_{k}\overset{d}{=}\mu_{2}(\nu_{k})$ on a common probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ where the positive finite Borel measures $\nu_{k}$ is supported on $I_{k}:=\left(-\frac{1}{k},-\frac{1}{k+1}\right]\cup\left[\frac{1}{k+1},\frac{1}{k}\right)$ 1313 13 We follow the convention that $\frac{1}{0}=\infty$ here to also include the case $k=0$ for $\nu_{0}$ .. As a consequence of Kolmogorov three series theorem, it is necessary and sufficient that $\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}}\mathbb{E}\big[\left(X_{k}-\mathbb{E}[X_{k}]\right)^{2}\big]<\infty$ , for the infinite series representation to converge almost surely. Moreover, $\mathbb{E}[X_{k}]=\int x\nu_{k}(dx)$ , $\mathbb{E}\big[\left(X_{k}-\mathbb{E}[X_{k}]\right)^{2}\big]=\int x^{2}\nu_{k}(dx)$ , and $\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}}\mathbb{E}\big[\left(X_{k}-\mathbb{E}[X_{k}]\right)^{2}\big]<\infty\leftrightarrow\int x^{2}d\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}}\nu_{k}(x)<\infty\leftrightarrow\int(x^{2}\wedge 1)d\nu(x)<\infty$ where $\nu=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}}\nu_{k}$ is the canonical measure of the infinitely divisible distribution $\mu$ Klenke (2008).

### 2.5 Resolution of the $s^{2}=2k$ conjecture

One of the major conclusions of the Dong et al. (2022) paper was that under the limit of large number of compositions of private mechanisms, a natural baseline trade-off function is the Gaussian trade-off function $f=T\left(N\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right),N\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)\right)$ for some $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ . But, as we saw earlier in 2.3 that this framework does not capture the Poisson example $f=T(P(\lambda_{1}),P(\lambda_{2}))$ . We show that under the limit of large number of compositions of private mechanisms, an enumeration of all the baseline trade-off functions (encompassing both Gaussian and Poisson case) is given by the following.

$$ \mathcal{I}_{T}=\{f=T(P,Q):P\in\mathcal{I}\text{ and }dQ(x)=e^{x}dP(x)\} $$

#### Theorem 3.

Consider the infinitely divisible distribution $P\overset{d}{=}-k+|s|Z$ with only Gaussian component $Z\sim N(0,1),k,s\in\mathbb{R}$ . If $dQ(x)=e^{x}dP(x)$ is a probability measure, then $s^{2}=2k$ . More precisely, for a Gaussian $P\in\mathcal{I}$ so that its Esscher tilt $dQ(x)=e^{x}dP(x)$ is a probability measure and $T(P,Q)\in\mathcal{I}_{f}$ if and only if $P=N\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)$ .

#### Proof.

The proof follows immediately from a computation of the moment-generating function of a Gaussian distribution, saying that $1=Q(\mathbb{R})=\mathbb{E}_{P}[\exp(x)]=\exp\left({-k+\frac{s^{2}}{2}}\right)\rightarrow s^{2}=2k$ . ∎

Now, in the following lemma, we describe the basic properties of trade-off functions in general and show that the class of infinitely divisible trade-off functions $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{T}}$ that captures both the Gaussian $T\left(N(0,1),N(\mu,1)\right)$ and the Poisson $T(P(\lambda_{1}),P(\lambda_{2}))$ trade-off functions.

#### Lemma 4.

Closure of trade-off functions under bijections and likelihood-ratios.

- 1. For two random variables defined $X,Y$ on some probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ and constants $0\neq c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}$ we have $T(X,Y)=T(c_{1}X+c_{2},c_{1}Y+c_{2})$ , where we denote for any random elements $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\overset{A,B}{\to}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}})$ trade-off function $T(A,B):=T(P_{A},P_{B})$ with $P_{A}=\mathbb{P}\circ A^{-1}$ , $P_{B}=\mathbb{P}\circ B^{-1}$ are the corresponding distributions. More generally, for any bijective measurable map $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}})\overset{h}{\to}(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}})$ we have $T(A,B)=T(h(A),h(B))$ .

- 2. For any two probability distributions $P,Q$ on some measurable space $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}})$ we have $T(P,Q)=T(L_{P},L_{Q})$ , where $L_{P}:=P\circ\left(\log\frac{dQ}{dP}\right)^{-1},L_{Q}:=Q\circ\left(\log\frac{dQ}{dP}\right)^{-1}$ are the distributions of the likelihood ratio $\log\frac{dQ}{dP}$ under their respective probability measures.

- 3. Gaussian We observe that if $P\overset{d}{=}N\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)$ , then $dQ(x)=e^{x}dP(x)\overset{d}{=}N\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)$ . So, the Gaussian trade-off curve as observed in Dong et al. (2022) belongs to $\mathcal{I}_{T}$ .

- 4. Poisson. The Poisson curve $T(P(\lambda_{1}),P(\lambda_{2}))\in\mathcal{I}_{T}$ , since $T(P,Q)=T(P(\lambda_{1}),P(\lambda_{2})$ , where $P\overset{d}{=}\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}+N\log\left(\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}\right)$ , with $N\sim P(\lambda_{1})$ and $dQ(x)=e^{x}dP(x)$ .

#### Proof.

- 1. Observe that from Blackwell’s theorem Dong et al. (2022) post-processing always increases the trade-off function. Therefore, for any measurable functions $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}})\overset{h}{\to}(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}})$ , we have $T(h(A),h(B))\geq T(A,B)$ . Moreover, if $h$ is bijective, reversing the process above yields $T(h(A),h(B))\geq T(h^{-1}(h(A)),h^{-1}(h(B)))=T(A,B)$ . Now, for scalar (or even vector) valued random variables, scaling $(x\to c_{1}x,c_{1}\neq 0)$ and translations $(x\to x+c_{2})$ are measurable bijections, and hence the equality.

- 2. Let $X\sim P$ , $Y\sim Q$ for random variables $X,Y$ on some probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ . Again, by post–processing, $T\big(L(X),L(Y)\big)\geq T(X,Y)=T(P,Q)$ . Now, for the reverse inequality, we apply the Neyman–Pearson likelihood ratio test (2) for the pair $(P,Q)$ of size $\alpha$ .

$$ \varphi^{*}(w):=\mathbf{1}\left(\log\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}\right)>\log\tau^{*}\right)+\lambda^{*}\mathbf{1}\left(\log\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}\right)=\log\tau^{*}\right),L=\log\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}\right) $$

with $\frac{dQ}{dP}:=\frac{dQ}{d\mu}/\frac{dP}{d\mu}:(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}})\to[0,\infty]$ , where the thresholds $\tau^{*}\in[0,\infty],\lambda^{*}\in[0,1]$ are chosen as in (2) so that $\mathbb{E}_{P}[\varphi^{*}]=\alpha$ . $$ \alpha=\mathbb{E}_{P}[\varphi^{*}]=\mathbb{E}_{P}\!\big[\mathbf{1}\{L>t^{*}\}+\lambda^{*}\,\mathbf{1}\{L=t^{*}\}\big]=P\!\big[L>t^{*}\big]+\lambda^{*}P\!\big[L=t^{*}\big], $$

(19)

$$ T(X,Y)(\alpha)=T(P,Q)(\alpha)=1-\mathbb{E}_{Q}[\varphi^{*}]=1-{Q}\!\big[L>t^{*}\big]-\lambda^{*}Q\big[L=t^{*}\}\big]. $$

(20) Now, consider the trade-off function between $P_{X}\overset{d}{=}L(X)$ and $P_{Y}\overset{d}{=}L(Y)$ with the test $\varphi^{*}(x)=\mathbf{1}\{x>t^{*}\}+\lambda^{*}\,\mathbf{1}\{x=t^{*}\}$ to have the type $I$ error $\mathbb{E}_{P_{X}}[\varphi^{*}]=\alpha$ and type II error $T(L(X),L(Y))(\alpha)\leq 1-\mathbb{E}_{P_{Y}}[\varphi^{*}]=T(X,Y)(\alpha)$ . Now, in the following lemma, we describe the basic properties of infinitely divisible trade-off functions, from which a closure of $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{T}}$ under pointwise limits $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{T}}\supset f_{n}\to f\in\mathcal{I}_{T}$ can also be inferred.

#### Lemma 5.

Basic properties of the infinitely divisible trade-off functions.

- 1. Tensor product. Consider $P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathcal{I}$ with their corresponding Esscher tilts $Q_{1},Q_{2}$ . Then the tensor product $f=T(P_{1}\otimes P_{2},Q_{1}\otimes Q_{2})=T(P,Q)\in\mathcal{I}_{T}$ with $P=P_{1}*P_{2}$ and $dQ=e^{x}dP$ . This immediately extends to $(P_{i},Q_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ for $P_{i}\in\mathcal{I}$ for any $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ as well.

- 2. Infinite divisibility. For any trade off function $f=T(P,Q)\in\mathcal{I}_{T}$ and any $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ there exists a trade off function $f_{n}=T(P_{n},Q_{n})\in\mathcal{I}_{T}$ such that $f=f_{n}^{\otimes n}$ .

#### Proof.

- 1. Observe that the likelihood ratio of the tensor product pairs of distributions satisfies

$$ L_{P_{1}\otimes P_{2}}:=(P_{1}\otimes P_{2})\circ\left(\log\frac{dQ_{1}\otimes Q_{2}}{dP_{1}\otimes P_{2}}\right)^{-1}=P_{1}*P_{2}=:P,\text{ and} $$

(22)

$$ dL_{Q_{1}\otimes Q_{2}}=d(Q_{1}\otimes Q_{2})\circ\log\left(\frac{dQ_{1}\otimes Q_{2}}{dP_{1}\otimes dP_{2}}\right)^{-1}=e^{x}dP_{1}*P_{2}=e^{x}dP=:dQ. $$

(23) Now, using the lemma above, we have $T(P_{1}\otimes P_{2},Q_{1}\otimes Q_{2})=T(L_{P_{1}\otimes P_{2}},L_{Q_{1}\otimes Q_{2}})=T(P,Q)$ . Finally, observe that $P_{1}*P_{2}$ is infinitely divisible if $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are Kallenberg (2021) since the addition of two independent infinitely divisible random variables is also an infinitely divisible random variable. Moreover, $\mathbb{E}_{P_{1}*P_{2}}[\exp(x)]=\mathbb{E}_{P_{1}}[\exp(x)]\mathbb{E}_{P_{2}}[\exp(x)]=1$ satisfies the normalization requirement.

- 2. Observe that by the definition of infinite divisibility of $P\overset{d}{=}X$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}_{P}[\exp(x)]=\mathbb{E}[\exp(X)]=1$ , for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ we have $P=P_{n}^{*n}$ for some probability measure $P_{n}$ on $(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})$ such that $1=\mathbb{E}_{P}[\exp(x)]=\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}[\exp(x)]\right)^{n}$ . Then, from the positivity of the quantity $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}[\exp(x)]>0$ , we have $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}[\exp(x)]=1$ , and so $dQ_{n}=e^{x}dP_{n}$ is a probability measure. Moreover, from the Levy-Khintchine characterization $(m,\sigma,\nu)$ of the characteristic function $\hat{P}(t)$ of an infinitely divisible distribution $P$ , it follows that $P_{n}$ itself is an infinitely divisible distribution with its Levy-Khintchine triplet $\left(\frac{m}{n},\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\frac{\nu}{n}\right)$ . Now, $f_{n}^{\otimes n}=T(P_{n}^{\otimes n},Q_{n}^{\otimes n})=T(P,Q)$ , where $P=P_{n}^{*n}$ , and $dQ=e^{x}dP$ .

## 3 Technical results

In this section, we prove the main technical result of the paper, establishing why is the collection of infinitely divisible trade-off functions $\mathcal{I}_{T}$ (18) appears under the limit of a large number of compositions of (nearly perfect) differentially private mechanisms, as a converse of the result 5.

#### Theorem 6.

Consider a sequence of trade off functions $\{f_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}}$ such that $f_{n}(0)=1$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ and $f_{n}^{\otimes n}(\alpha)\to f_{\infty}(\alpha)$ pointwise on $[0,1]$ for some trade-off function $f_{\infty}$ (1), then $f_{\infty}$ is an infinitely divisible trade off function. More precisely $f_{\infty}\in\mathcal{I}_{T}$ .

#### Proof.

We prove it in a few steps. Blackwell-Le-Cam equivalence. Observe that our conditions of Theorem 6 only involve trade-off functions $\{f_{n}:n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\},f$ , and it is deliberate since the definition of $f$ -differential privacy of a mechanism 2 does not involve any details of the binary experiment $\mathcal{E}=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P,Q)$ , except that it works for any such equivalent representation of the baseline trade-off function $f$ through $f=T(P,Q)$ . This relates to the Blackwell-Le Cam equivalence of experiments, which we will briefly describe for binary experiments with a parameter set $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ consisting of two elements.

Given two binary experiments $\mathcal{E}_{1}=(\Omega_{1},\mathcal{F}_{1},P_{1},Q_{1})$ , $\mathcal{E}_{2}=(\Omega_{2},\mathcal{F}_{2},P_{2},Q_{2})$ , a notion of distance between $\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2}$ (better known as Le-Cam deficiency) was defined in Le Cam (1986) that is given as

$$ \textbf{Le-Cam distance: }\Delta(\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2})=\max(\delta(\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2}),\delta(\mathcal{E}_{2},\mathcal{E}_{1})),\text{ where} $$

$$ \textbf{Le-Cam deficiency: }\delta(\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2})=\inf_{R:(\Omega_{1},\mathcal{F}_{1})\to(\Omega_{2},\mathcal{F}_{2})}\max(\|RP_{1}-P_{2}\|_{1},\|RQ_{1}-Q_{2}\|_{1}), $$

where the infimum is taken over all (appropriate) Markov kernels $R$ and for a pair of probability measures $\mu_{1},\mu_{2}$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_{2})$ , $\|\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}\|_{1}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal{F}_{2}}|\mu_{1}(A)-\mu_{2}(A)|$ is the total variation distance.

One of the key results of Le Cam (1986), Torgersen (1991) is that $\Delta(\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2})=0$ if and only if $f_{1}:=T(P_{1},Q_{1})\equiv T(P_{2},Q_{2})=:f_{2}$ . Moreover, $f_{2}\geq f_{1}$ if and only if $\delta(\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2})=0$ if and only if there exists a Markov kernel $R:(\Omega_{1},\mathcal{F}_{1})\to(\Omega_{2},\mathcal{F}_{2})$ such that $RP_{1}=P_{2}$ and $RQ_{1}=Q_{2}.$ Furthermore, the correspondence $\mathcal{E}=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P,\mathcal{Q})\leftrightarrow f=T(P,Q)$ preserves the Le-Cam distance in the following sense and therefore is quantitative, since Torgersen (1991)[Corollary 9.3.27] states

$$ \sqrt{2}\Delta(\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2})=\Lambda(Q^{(1)},Q^{(2)}),\text{ where the } $$

cumulative distribution functions $F^{(1)},F^{(2)}$ of probability measures $Q^{(1)},Q^{(2)}$ on $[0,1]$ are given

$$ \text{by }Q^{(i)}[0,\alpha]=1-f_{i}(\alpha)\text{ for }\alpha\in(0,1]\text{ and }Q^{(i)}[\{0\}]=(1-f_{i}(0)),\text{ for }i\in\{1,2\} $$

and $\Lambda(Q^{(1)},Q^{(2)})$ denotes the Levy distance between the probability measures $Q^{(1)},Q^{(2)}$ through their cumulative distribution functions $F^{(1)},F^{(2)}$ on $[0,1]$ as Kallenberg (2021)

$$ \Lambda(F^{(1)},F^{(2)})=\inf\{\varepsilon>0:F^{(2)}(x-\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\leq F^{(1)}(x)\leq F^{(2)}(x+\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\text{ for all }x\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]\}. $$

The key observations about the Levy-distance $\Lambda(\cdot,\cdot)$ (hence $\Delta$ for binary $\Theta$ ) is that it precisely captures convergence in distribution. More precisely, our assumption in Theorem 6 about the pointwise convergence of $f_{n}^{\otimes n}\to f_{\infty}$ on $[0,1]$ 2424 24 The assumption $f_{n}(0)=1$ (hence $f_{\infty}(0)=1$ ) is there to ensure that $Q_{\infty}\ll P_{\infty}$ for $f_{\infty}=T(P_{\infty},Q_{\infty}).$ is the equivalent to the condition that $\Delta(1-f_{n}^{\otimes n},1-f_{\infty})\to 0$ , and therefore captures the meaning of convergence of experiments $\Delta(\mathcal{E}_{n}^{\otimes n},\mathcal{E}_{\infty})\to 0$ where the correspondence $\mathcal{E}_{n}\equiv(P_{n},Q_{n})\to f_{n}=T(P_{n},Q_{n})$ and $\mathcal{E}_{\infty}\equiv(P_{n},Q_{n})\to f_{\infty}\equiv T(P_{\infty},Q_{\infty})$ .

From the definition of $\Delta(\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2})$ , given a fixed parameter set $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ (in our case) one can (consistently) define a equivalence class of experiments $[\mathcal{E}]:=\{\mathcal{E}_{1}:\Delta(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{E}_{1})=0\}$ with the same trade-off curve $f\leftrightarrow[\mathcal{E}]$ . Now, in the $f$ -differential privacy framework of Dong et al. (2022), it only depends on the equivalence classes of experiments and not the exact representation, such as $f=T(P,Q)$ . However, this explicit representation $f=T(P,Q)$ is important in practice since, one has to implement a Markov kernel (a generalized noise-adding mechanism) such as adding Gaussian noise to achieve Gaussian differential privacy $f=T(N(0,1)N(\mu,1))$ .

This is the reason our explicit parametrization of infinitely divisible trade-off functions $f_{\infty}=T(P_{\infty},Q_{\infty})$ of $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{T}}$ is important, and we will demonstrate in section 4 how to achieve infinitely divisible privacy for a large class of infinitely divisible trade-off functions $f_{\infty}=T(P_{\infty},Q_{\infty})$ , including the practically relevant Poisson case $f_{\infty}=T(P(\lambda_{1}),P(\lambda_{2}))$ .

Large deviation regime versus infinitely divisible regime. Instead of a sequence $\{f_{n}:n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\}$ of trade-off functions and considering their tensor product $f_{n}^{\otimes n}$ , if one takes a single trade-off function $f$ (independent of $n$ ) and considers $f^{\otimes n}$ , one has a large deviation principle

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log f^{\otimes n}(\alpha)=\int_{0}^{z_{f}}\log|f^{\prime}(x)|dx,\text{ for all }\alpha\in(0,1) $$

where $z_{f}=f^{-1}(0)$ is the first zero of $f$ , where $f^{-1}$ is the generalized inverse of $f$ (4) (seeDong et al. (2022)[Prop B.4], Polyanskiy and Wu (2025), Torgersen (1991)). Although our focus is on the infinitely divisible (central limit) regime, where there is some non-trivial privacy left even after a large number of nearly perfect private operations. The large deviation regime is also of interest and has been used in the theoretical development of watermark detection for LLMs Li et al. (2025).

#### Proposition 1 (More infinitely divisible limits).

Given trade-off functions $\{f^{(n)},g^{(n)}:n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\}$

$$ \text{If }f^{(n)}\to f_{\infty}\in\mathcal{T}\text{ and }g^{(n)}\to g_{\infty}\in\mathcal{T}\text{ poinwise }\text{ then }f^{(n)}\otimes g^{(n)}\to f_{\infty}\otimes g_{\infty}\in\mathcal{T}. $$

First, recall that the pointwise convergence of monotone functions $\{f^{(n)}\}_{n}(\{g^{(n)}\}_{n})$ mapping $[0,1]\to[0,1]$ to a limiting monotone continuous function $f_{\infty}(g_{\infty})$ mapping $[0,1]\to[0,1]$ implies uniform convergence on $[0,1]$ , and so we analyze under $\|h_{1}-h_{2}\cdot\|_{\infty}^{[0,1]}=\sup\{h_{1}(x)-h_{2}(x):x\in[0,1]\}$ . This follows from the ‘trick’ $|G(a_{n},b_{n})-G(a,b)|=|G(a_{n},b_{n})-G(a_{n},b)+G(a_{n},b)-G(a,b)|$

Therefore, to fit with the $f$ -DP framework of Dong et al. $$ g=\min\{f,f^{-1}\}^{**}(x)=\begin{cases}f^{-1}(x),&x\in[0,f(\bar{x})],\\[3.0pt]

The utility of the $f$ -differential privacy framework of Dong et al. (2022) lies in the ability to choose the baseline $f$ based on the class of problems at hand. ## 5 Neyman-Pearson lemma under a coarser $\sigma$ -algebra

The Neyman-Pearson optimizer $\varphi^{*}$ of the trade-off function $T(P,Q)$ for probability measures $(P,Q)$ on a measurable space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ involves the likelihood ratio (Radon-Nikodym derivative) random variable $F=\frac{dQ}{dP}:(\Omega,\mathcal{F})\to[0,\infty]$ (2), but we pose a natural question: what happens when we shrink the original $\sigma$ -algebra $\mathcal{F}$ to a smaller one $\mathcal{G}$ 6767 67 Shrinking the $\sigma$ -algebra to a smaller $\sigma$ algebra captures the intuition of blurring the information in subsets of the sample space $\Omega$ by reducing the number of allowed subsets from $\mathcal{F}$ to $\mathcal{G}$ . A complementary way would be to say that coarsening information is the same as testing with fewer allowed observables $\varphi$ , which are available at our disposal. See Revuz and Yor (1999) for more details on the intuition behind filtration of $\sigma$ -algebras., so that the Radon-Nikodym derivative $H=\frac{dQ}{dP}$ is not a $\mathcal{G}$ measurable random variable; therefore, $\varphi^{*}$ cannot be the Neyman-Pearson optimizer for $(P,Q)$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal{G})$ . In this section, we answer this question in full generality. Our motivation comes from a Bayesian perspective of differential privacy as proposed in Strack and Yang (2024), whose connections with the $f$ -DP framework will also be an interesting future direction.

#### Theorem 22.

Consider a measurable space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ , and let $P,Q$ be probability measures on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ 6868 68 We do not need this assumption of absolute continuity of $Q\ll P$ , and the result holds more generally when we extend our definition of the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\frac{dQ}{dP}:=\frac{dQ}{d\mu}/\frac{dP}{d\mu}$ for a dominating $2\mu=P+Q$ .. Denote the likelihood ratio $F:=\frac{dQ}{dP}:(\Omega,\mathcal{F})\to[0,\infty]$ (defined only $P$ -almost surely). Let $\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ be a sub- $\sigma$ -algebra (a coarsening), and $P^{\mathcal{G}}$ and $Q^{\mathcal{G}}$ are the restrictions of $P,Q$ to $\mathcal{G}$ . Define the conditional likelihood ratio $G\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{P}\!\left[F\,\middle|\,\mathcal{G}\right]:(\Omega,\mathcal{G})\to[0,\infty]$ . Then,

- • $G$ is (a $P^{\mathcal{G}}$ -almost sure version of) the Radon–Nikodym derivative $\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal{G})$ .

Now, consider the coarsened trade-off function $T_{\mathcal{G}}(P,Q)\equiv T(P^{\mathcal{G}},Q^{\mathcal{G}}):[0,1]\to[0,1]$ defined as

$$ T(P^{\mathcal{G}},Q^{\mathcal{G}})(\alpha)=\inf_{\varphi}\Bigl\{\mathbb{E}_{Q}[1-\varphi]\,\Bigm|\,\mathbb{E}_{P}[\varphi]\leq\alpha,\;\varphi:(\Omega,\mathcal{G})\!\to[0,1]\text{ measurable}\Bigr\}. $$

- • The Neyman-Pearson optimizer $\varphi_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}$ achieving $T_{\mathcal{G}}(P,Q)$ at level $\alpha\in[0,1]$ is given by (2)

$$ \varphi^{*}(w):=\mathbf{1}\left(\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}>\tau^{*}\right)+\lambda^{*}\mathbf{1}\left(\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}=\tau^{*}\right),\quad\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}:=\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{d\mu^{G}}/\frac{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}{d\mu^{\mathcal{G}}}:(\Omega,\mathcal{G})\to[0,\infty] $$

for $2\mu^{\mathcal{G}}=P^{\mathcal{G}}+Q^{\mathcal{G}}$ , the ratios of Radon–Nikodym derivatives, and $\tau^{*},\lambda^{*}$ are determined by choosing $\tau^{*}\in[0,\infty]$ as the unique number

such that $P^{\mathcal{G}}\left(\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}\geq\tau^{*}\right)\geq\alpha\geq P^{\mathcal{G}}\left(\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}>\tau^{*}\right)$ ,

$$ \lambda^{*}:=\frac{\alpha-P^{\mathcal{G}}\left(\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}>\tau^{*}\right)}{P^{\mathcal{G}}\left(\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}\geq\tau^{*}\right)-P^{\mathcal{G}}\left(\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}>\tau^{*}\right)}\mathbf{1}\left(\alpha-P^{\mathcal{G}}\left(\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}>\tau^{*}\right)>0\right)\text{ so }\mathbb{E}_{P}[\varphi_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}]=\alpha. $$

- • Moreover, the trade-off function satisfies data-processing inequality (Blackwell ordering)

$$ T(P^{\mathcal{G}},Q^{\mathcal{G}})(\alpha)\;\geq\;T(P,Q)(\alpha)\text{ for all }\alpha\in[0,1],\text{ with equality for all }\alpha\text{ if and only if } $$

$F$ itself is $\mathcal{G}$ -measurable $P$ almost surely or equivalently, $\mathbb{E}_{P}[F|\mathcal{G}]=F$ , $P$ almost surely6969 69 A complementary way is to say that the information $\mathcal{G}$ is sufficient for the binary experiment $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P,Q)$ ..

#### Proof.

First, we show that $G$ is the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}$ . Now, observe that for any measurable function $(\Omega,\mathcal{G})\overset{\varphi}{\to}[0,1]$ , we have $\mathbb{E}_{Q}[\varphi]=\mathbb{E}_{P}[F\,\varphi]=\mathbb{E}_{P}\!\big[\,\mathbb{E}_{P}(F\mid\mathcal{G})\,\varphi\,\big]=\mathbb{E}_{P}[G\,\varphi].$

Second, the constrained minimization of $\mathbb{E}_{Q}[1-\varphi]$ over $\mathcal{G}$ -measurable $\varphi$ with $\mathbb{E}_{P}[\varphi]\leq\alpha$ reduces to the standard Neyman-Pearson problem for the reduced experiment $(\Omega,\mathcal{G},P^{\mathcal{G}},Q^{\mathcal{G}})$ with likelihood ratio $\frac{dQ^{\mathcal{G}}}{dP^{\mathcal{G}}}$ . The Neyman-Pearson lemma (108) gives the threshold form of $\varphi_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}$ .

Finally, the inequality $T(P^{\mathcal{G}},Q^{\mathcal{G}})\geq T(P,Q)$ follows immediately because $\varphi:(\Omega,\mathcal{G})\to[0,1]$ is measurable implies $\varphi:(\Omega,\mathcal{F})\to[0,1]$ is measurable. Moreover, if $\mathbb{E}_{P}[F|\mathcal{G}]=F$ , then $\varphi_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}=\varphi^{*}$ in (108) and hence equality holds for all $\alpha$ holds. Conversely, equality holds at all $\alpha\in[0,1]$ , by the uniqueness of Neyman-Pearson optimizer, $\varphi_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}=\varphi^{*}$ at all $\alpha$ , and therefore $F=\frac{dQ}{dP}$ itself is $\mathcal{G}$ measurable7070 70 By the restriction of $\varphi^{*}_{\mathcal{G}}=\varphi^{*}$ at all $\alpha\in[0,1]$ , we need $\{F>\tau\}_{\tau\geq 0}$ and $\{F=\tau\}_{\tau\geq 0}$ to be $\mathcal{G}$ measurable, and therefore $F$ itself is $G$ measurable, since it is by definition non-negative.. So, $G=\mathbb{E}_{P}[F|\mathcal{G}]=F,P$ almost surely. ∎

As a consequence, we have $F_{\mu}(n)\leq F_{n}\leq F_{\mu}(n+1)\leq F_{n+1}\leq F_{\mu}(n+2)$ for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ .

So the Neyman-Pearson optimizer on $(\Omega,\mathcal{G})\equiv(\mathbb{Z},2^{\mathbb{Z}})$ is a threshold in $N$ 7676 76 To follow the theorem 22, one could equivalently threshold at the value based on $F_{n}$ as well. (along with some randomization as required). For the non-randomized part, consider an threshold $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ ,

$$ \text{type I error}=\alpha_{k}:=P(N\geq k)=\sum_{n\geq k}p_{n}=1-\Phi(k),\text{ and } $$

$$ \text{type II error}=T_{\mathcal{G}}(P,Q)(\alpha_{k}):=Q(N<k)=\sum_{n<k}q_{n}=\Phi(k-\mu). $$

Thus, the trade-off function $T_{\mathcal{G}}(P^{\mathcal{G}},Q^{\mathcal{G}})$ at the points with type I errors $\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\subset[0,1]$ 7777 77 These are the values of type I errors which do not require randomization in Neyman-Pearson lemma., have the respective minimum value of type II errors as $\{\Phi(k-\mu)\big)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ or equivalently as the subset of points $\{\alpha_{k},\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha_{k})-\mu)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\subset\{\alpha,T_{\mathcal{G}}(P,Q)(\alpha)\}_{\alpha\in[0,1]}\subset[0,1]^{2}$ . Now, to have the entire $T_{\mathcal{G}}(P,Q)$ , one linearly interpolates the points above on the curve. More precisely, for any $\alpha\in[\alpha_{k+1},\,\alpha_{k}]$ , define $\varphi_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}(N)=\mathbf{1}(N>k)+\lambda^{*}\mathbf{1}(N=k),$ where $\lambda^{*}\in[0,1]$ is given by

$$ \lambda^{*}=\frac{\alpha-\alpha_{k+1}}{\alpha_{k}-\alpha_{k+1}},\text{ and }T_{\mathcal{G}}(P,Q)(\alpha)\;=\;T_{\mathcal{G}}(P,Q)(\alpha_{k+1})-\lambda^{*}\,q_{k}. $$

∎

This finishes the description of the computation of the trade-off function $T_{\mathcal{G}}(P,Q)$ for a Gaussian shift family, which is clearly equal to $T(P,Q)$ at the points of type $I$ errors $\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ without requiring randomization, and linear interpolated otherwise. Therefore, it always lies above the original Gaussian trade-off curve $T(P,Q)$ . Moreover, the $\mu<0$ , case be dealt in exactly similar way.

## 6 Conclusion and Future Work

In this paper, we introduce the hypothesis testing-based framework of infinitely divisible privacy 6, encompassing both the Gaussian differential privacy of Dong et al. (2022) and the newly proposed Poisson differential privacy 9, which are not just natural baselines for count statistics but also appear under repeated compositions of (nearly perfect) differentially private outputs. Along the way, we resolve the $s^{2}=2k$ conjecture of Dong et al. (2022) as a consequence of contiguity 3.

In practice, the number of private operations made on a dataset is uncertain. We show that under randomization of the number of operations, the limiting trade-off can even escape the universal class of infinitely divisible trade-off functions 64 We illustrate this with a locally asymptotically mixed normal (LAMN) example (66), following the spirit of Le Cam (1986).

Then, we construct a mechanism in Theorem 13 that optimally attains (asymmetric) Poisson differential privacy for real-valued statistics, including count statistics, thus going beyond standard additive-noise mechanisms. Afterwards, we demonstrate that Poisson baselines naturally appear for graph-based datasets, where released statistics are inherently discretized 20.

Finally, inspired by a Bayesian perspective on DP (Strack and Yang, 2024), we quantify exactly how trade-off functions degrade under information coarsening and derive a coarsened Neyman-Pearson lemma 22 with equality characterizations via conditional likelihood ratios 22. We demonstrate this by explicitly working out the Gaussian case 2 that extends to symmetric-log concave family.

Several interesting directions follow, and many have been detailed in the remarks within the text. First, our algorithmic result suggests the construction of private mechanisms that are optimal with respect to a given natural, infinitely divisible trade-off curve. Second, it would be extremely interesting to illustrate the tightness of the proposed Poisson differential privacy framework on graph-based problems of modern interest Karwa and Slavković (2016). Third, it would be interesting to analyze how privacy degrades when one is allowed to stop adaptively. Finally, it would be fascinating to find an equivalence between the $f$ -differential privacy framework of Dong et al. (2022) based on comparison of trade-off functions and the (Bayesian) framework of privacy-preserving signals Strack and Yang (2024), since coarsening the underlying $\sigma$ algebra clarifies how information restrictions lead to an increase in indistinguishability.

## Appendix A Supplementary material

We first define a Markov kernel (randomized mechanism) following Kallenberg (2021).

#### Definition 7 (Markov kernel).

Let $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}})$ and $(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}})$ be measurable spaces. A Markov kernel (also called a stochastic kernel or transition kernel) from $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}})$ to $(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}})$ is a map

$$ K:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}\to[0,1],\text{ usually written }K(x,B)\text{ for }x\in\mathcal{X},B\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}, $$

such that for every fixed $x\in X$ , the set function $B\mapsto K(x,B)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}})$ . Moreover, for every fixed $B\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{Y}}$ , the function $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{X}}$ -measurable.

We state the following Berry Esseen CLT, where $\mathbf{kl}$ denotes the vector $(\operatorname{kl}(f_{1}),\ldots,\operatorname{kl}(f_{n}))$ and $\bm{\kappa}_{2}$ , $\bm{\kappa}_{3}$ , $\overline{\bm{\kappa}}_{3}$ are defined similarly; in addition, $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ and $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ are the $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ norms, respectively.

Our first lemma summarizes some of the basic but extremely fruitful properties of the Gaussian trade-off function $f_{G,\varepsilon}(x)=T(N(0,1),N(\varepsilon,1))(x)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1-x)-\varepsilon)$ for all $x\in[0,1]$ , and any $\varepsilon\geq 0$ . Among others, it proves that $T\left(N\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right),N\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{2},\mu^{2}\right)\right)=f_{G,|\mu|}$ for any $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ .

#### Lemma 23.

(Dong et al. (2022)) The Gaussian trade off functions satisfy the following properties:

- • Monotonicity: For any pair $\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2}\geq 0$ , $\varepsilon_{1}\leq\varepsilon_{2}$ if and only if

$$ f_{G,\varepsilon_{1}}(x)\geq f_{G,\varepsilon_{2}}(x)\text{ for all }x\in[0,1]. $$

(120)

- • Closure under suprema: For any collection of $(\varepsilon_{i})_{i\in I}\subset\mathbb{R}$ with index set $I$

$$ \inf_{i\in I}f_{G,\varepsilon_{i}}(x)=f_{G,\sup_{i\in I}\varepsilon_{i}}(x)\text{ for all }x\in[0,1] $$

(121)

- • Symmetry: For any $\mu_{1},\nu_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ and $\sigma>0$

$$ T(\nu_{2}+\sigma N(0,\mathbb{I}_{p}),\mu_{1}+\sigma N(0,\mathbb{I}_{p}))=T(\mu_{1}+\sigma N(0,I_{p}),\nu_{2}+\sigma N(0,I_{p})) $$

(122)

- • Dimension freeness: For any $\mu_{1},\nu_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ and $\Sigma\succ 0$ let $\varepsilon^{2}:=\langle(\mu_{1}-\nu_{2}),\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_{1}-\nu_{2})\rangle$ . Then

$$ T(\mu_{1}+\sqrt{\Sigma}N(0,\mathbb{I}_{p}),\nu_{2}+\sqrt{\Sigma}N(0,\mathbb{I}_{p}))\equiv T(N(0,1),N(\varepsilon,1)), $$

(123)

Intuition and importance: The proof of this lemma is immediate from the explicit description of $f_{G,\varepsilon}(x)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1-x)-\varepsilon)$ where $\Phi(\cdot)$ is the CDF of a standard Gaussian variable $\Phi(t)=\mathbb{P}[N(0,1)\leq t]$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ . It also requires applying the Neyman-Pearson lemma or the likelihood ratio test Polyanskiy and Wu (2025). But, the conclusions that they imply are extremely powerful.

Monotonicity: The monotonicity condition (120) reduces an apriori difficult functional comparison between two functions $f$ and $g$ at uncountably many points to a comparison of just one parameter $\varepsilon$ .

Closure under suprema: The closure under suprema property (121) essentially says two very important things. First, it makes it easy to identify what the suprema of an apriori arbitrary collection of functions $\{f_{i}\}_{i}$ is (in fact explicitly). Second, the limiting object is a function of the same kind: it is again a Gaussian trade-off function with a different choice of parameter $\varepsilon$ .

Symmetry: The symmetry property (122) (requires Neyman-Pearson lemma) is very interesting because the definition of a trade-off function $T(P,Q)$ 1 is asymmetric in general, between its first and second arguments. But, for a pair of shifted isotropic Gaussians, they match because of the spherical symmetry (orthogonal invariance) of the standard Gaussian density in any dimension.

Dimension freeness: The dimension freeness property (123) (requires Neyman-Pearson lemma) makes the case for Gaussian certifiability in high dimensions stronger than any other notion of certifiability. This is because, almost all the results of classical statistics that are true in low dimensions, fail to hold in high dimensions, because many of the quantities involved in controlling the errors are dimension dependent and blows up when $p\uparrow\infty$ . It is often the case that finding a dimension-free quantity or even an inequality that tensorizes 7878 78 We are referring dimension free Poincare and Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities of high-dimensional statistics that are extremely important in obtaining concentration bounds in high dimensions van Handel (2016). help us resolve high dimensional issues.

Our second lemma says that the some aspects of the Gaussian trade-off functions generalize.

#### Lemma 24.

Dong et al. (2022)[Lemma A.2, Proposition A.3] Consider a symmetric random variable $X\overset{d}{=}-X$ with CDF $F$ having a log-concave Lebesgue density. Consider its baseline trade-off function $f_{X,\varepsilon}(x)=T(X,\varepsilon+X)(x)$ for all $x\in[0,1]$ .

- 1. Symmetry: For any $t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\delta=|t_{2}-t_{1}|$ the following holds for all $x\in[0,1]$ .

$$ T(t_{1}+X,t_{2}+X)(x)=F\left(F^{-1}(1-x)-\delta\right)=T(t_{2}+X,t_{1}+X)(x). $$

(124)

$$ \text{So, }T(t_{1}+X,t_{2}+X)(x)=T(X,\delta+X)(x)=T(\delta+X,X)(x) $$

(125)

- 2. Monotonicity: For $\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2}\geq 0$ . Then $\varepsilon_{1}\leq\varepsilon_{2}$ if and only if

$$ f_{X,\varepsilon_{1}}(x)\geq f_{X,\varepsilon_{2}}(x)\text{ for all }x\in[0,1]. $$

(126)

Intuition and importance: The proof of this lemma is along the same lines of the proof given in Dong et al. (2022)[Lemma A.2, Proposition A.3]. Using log-concavity of the density of $X$ and symmetry $X\overset{d}{=}-X$ , there is an explicit description of $f_{X,\varepsilon}(x)=F(F^{-1}(1-x)-\varepsilon)$ where $F(\cdot)$ is the CDF of the random variable $X$ , $F(t)=\mathbb{P}[X\leq t]$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ , and $\varepsilon\geq 0$ .
